subsubtopic: PAKISTAN-PLEA FOR RELEASE OF TARIQ AHSAN, IMPRISONED UNIVERSITY STUDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two years ago a Carleton University Ph.D. student, Tariq Ahsan, was arrested and jailed in Pakistan for political reasons, on a trumped-up charge of possessing seditious material. After 17 months of imprisonment, Mr. Ahsan finally came to trial in April of this year. He was sentenced just last week to two years' hard labour, a sentence to begin at the trial, not even at the beginning of his imprisonment. Mr. Ahsan's physical condition was poor when he left Canada two years ago, and according to his family has worsened considerably while in prison. A sentence of two years' hard labour may be a death sentence for Mr. Ahsan.
Mr. Ahsan's teaching assistantship position is being held open for him at Carleton University, as well as additional scholarship funds. His colleagues in the political science department are anxious for his safe return to Canada.
This imprisonment constitutes a serious infringement on the most fundamental of civil liberties, and Members of all Parties and all levels of Government have already made their views known to the Government of Pakistan. Were Mr. Ahsan a Canadian citizen we could do more for him. What we can do, and what 1 urge all Members of this House to do, is to write to the Government of Pakistan and the Ambassador for Pakistan, appealing for Mr. Ahsan's release so he may return to Canada and continue his studies.

subsubtopic: CLOSING OF RADIO READING SERVICE IN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of the Special Committee on the Disabled and Handicapped I was shocked to learn recently that the Oakville-based radio reading service, which provided reading service for an estimated 3,000 blind and visually impaired persons, was forced off the air
because of the provincial Government's refusal to provide any further funding for the service.
The station, which used voluntary readers to broadcast verbatim in-depth accounts from newspapers and other readings, was itself a newspaper to the blind. Its broadcast area extended through the Golden Horseshoe, Scarborough, Guelph, and Kitchener, and as far away as Simcoe. Last year the station had its operation cut back from seven days to five days in an effort to extend its limited budget. However, this did little to ameliorate the problem of inadequate funding.
It is important that the federal Minister of State (Mr. Joyal) responsible for the status of the disabled meet his provincial counterpart to inquire into this matter and recommend that careful consideration be given to reinstating the radio reading service so that the visually handicapped persons who were able to take advantage of it can continue to function in a more complete way.

subsubtopic: REPORTING OF INCIDENTS IN OKANAGAN-SIMILKAMEEN AREA OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the CBC, in its program "The Journal", reported in a most irresponsible and inflammatory manner on a subject which deserves to be treated with sensitivity and understanding. People in the Okanagan-Similkameen area of British Columbia are incensed by the airing of unworthy statements which allege that they have a bad racist attitude, intolerance is institutionalized, that they practise harassment of minority groups such as Doukhobors, Chinese, Japanese, and now Quebecois, and that there is a hard core of really bigoted people in the area. I say shame to the CBC for a distorted sensationalization of a lamentable situation where tensions have arisen in certain communities between farm workers from Quebec and a minor provocative element, some of whom are also transient to the area.
[DOT] (mo)
The CBC highlighted untruths, and generalizations such as "Orchard workers are classed as no good", and "People think that transient workers are simply a bunch of dirty hippies", the inference that the rape of two girls from Quebec was racially motivated, and the implication that people who resent the action of one who urinated openly on a Main Street store front are displaying racial intolerance. The CBC contributes nothing by engaging in such objectionable programming.

subsubtopic: THE CASE OF DONALD MARSHALL-LEGAL EXPENSES OF COURT SYSTEM VICTIM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, both the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) and the Minister of Indian Affairs (Mr. Munro) are now saying that they cannot provide funds to cover the legal costs of Donald Marshall. Ministers of the Crown stand helpless in the face of a gross injustice done to a fellow Canadian.
Mr. Marshall spent 11 years in prison for a crime he did not commit. Whether or not this comes under provincial or federal jurisdiction becomes irrelevant in light of his unjust suffering. Mr. Marshall's punishment for a crime he did not commit is a stain on Canada's entire justice system. It is something about which all Canadians should feel ashamed.
Considering other cases, such as that of Susan Nelles, the subject of general compensation for victims of faulty court proceedings would make a good subject for this House to consider.
Mr. Marshall faces more than $80,000 in legal expenses. The Government does not need to be helpless. It can bring in a Bill to pay these costs. My Party promises to deal with any such Bill expeditiously. I am sure the Conservatives would also want to pass such a Bill with a minimum of debate. I urge the Government to take action and not to stand by helplessly in the face of injustice.

subsubtopic: THE CASE OF HUGH HAMBLETON-REPORTED OFFER OF PROSECUTION IMMUNITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am glad to see both the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) in the House. During his trial before the Old Bailey in the United Kingdom, a former CIDA official, Mr. Hugh Hambleton, a Canadian being tried on espionage charges for passing information to the KGB, admitted to having seen in Canada in April, 1980, official confirmation from the Department of Justice to the effect that he would not be prosecuted in Canada if he were to "co-operate" with Canadian security authorities in determining the exact nature of his contacts with the KGB. The existence of any such offer has since been denied by the Solicitor General.
It is time some clarification of this matter was provided to the Canadian public. Why did the Canadian security authorities make such an offer? Why was Hambleton allowed to travel freely to the United Kingdom where, obviously, he expected to defect? Why was he warned twice, once before leaving Canada and secondly upon arrival in the United Kingdom, that he would almost certainly be tried in Britain on charges of espionage under law identical to the Canadian Official Secrets Act? Who prevented the Canadian authorities from bringing charges?

-any person that is engaged directly or indirectly in, or controls or is controlled by a person that is engaged directly or indirectly in, the Atlantic Fisheries; "person" includes an individual, a body corporate, a partnership, an association, a trust, a cooperative and any trustee or legal representative thereof; "restructuring", in respect of a fishery enterprise, includes the reorganization, refinancing, modernization, rationalization and expansion of the enterprise, and any similar activity directed toward making the enterprise economically viable.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to facilitate the development of viable Atlantic fisheries that are competitive and privately-owned through the restructuring of certain fishery enterprises. That part of the Bill is something which is worthwhile and I can certainly support the objective of this Bill, but the Bill goes much too far in its powers.
As described in the Bill the powers are:
4.	(I) To carry out the purpose of this Act, the Minister may, on behalf of Her Majesty,
(a)	acquire, hold or dispose of or otherwise deal with shares, debentures or other securities of, or any security interest in, any fishery enterprise;
(b)	pledge, hypothecate or charge any share, debenture or other security, or other security interest, acquired or held under paragraph (a); and
(r) enter into any agreement or arrangement necessary or incidental to any activity referred to in paragraph (a) or (b).
The guarantees under Clause 6 are:
To carry out the purpose of this Act, the Minister may, with the approval of the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, on such terms and conditions as the Minister specifies, guarantee the repayment of any portion of the principal and interest owing on any loan made to a fishery enterprise.
(2) The aggregate amount of guarantees given under this section that are outstanding at any one time shall not exceed one hundred million dollars.
In Clause 7 the Minister is authorized to exercise specific powers:
The Governor in Council may by order authorize any minister of the Crown, other than the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, to exercise in respect of such fishery enterprise as is specified in the order such powers referred to in this Act as are specified in the order.
Mr. Speaker, that is a lot of jargon that is hard to understand. It is definitely difficult for me, as a layman, to understand the full implications. My understanding of this Bill is that it is going to give the Government, through the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) or some other designated Minister, complete control of the fishery in Atlantic Canada. There are many "anys" in the Bill. The Bill gives the Minister the power to buy, sell, trade or hold "any" sector of the fishing industry. It also gives the Minister the power to
loan or guarantee "any" amount of money to "any" fishery enterprise.
I will give you some background to the introduction of this Bill, Mr. Speaker. Due to the condition of the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced the appointment of a task force on Atlantic fisheries in January of 1982. The main purpose of this task force was to recommend "how to achieve and maintain a viable Atlantic fishing industry with due consideration for the overall economic and social development of the Atlantic Provinces". The Chairman of this task force, Mr. Michael Kirby, worked primarily with 11 other people in developing the Kirby report.
Mr. Speaker, the Kirby report is the most positive report seen in decades. It was presented as an interlocking package. The federal Government is threatening the integrity and future of the report by changing some of the recommendations. The federal Government seems to be picking, choosing and switching, to suit their needs, from a report which must be viewed as a whole package in order to be effective. In the Kirby report, in a section entitled "The Harvesting Sector", recommendations in the area of fishing licences are discussed. The federal Government must accept the licensing review process. This term should be explained as the process of licensing is currently political and controlled by the federal Government.
There are no written guidelines established for companies and fishermen to follow, should they wish to expand or develop their businesses. It is the damage done to the private sector fishing industry by many years of Liberal fisheries policies which has left no alternative but to restructure the industry. The Liberal Government has encouraged excessive expansion through federal improvement loans. It has shown political interference in licensing and capital expenditures. It has been inconsistent in policy areas and has not been effective in consultations with the Provinces.
The President of the Eastern Fisheries Federation expressed his concerns about the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada by stating that the use of Government incentives had ballooned in Nova Scotia's two largest companies to the point where so much money had to be made to stay afloat that the result is too much fish on the market. He feels that the fishing industry needs to be built by people who have an interest in the fishery rather than a bunch of bureaucrats.
So far under this restructuring, only large companies are being taken over and those companies not involved could find themselves penalized for their independence. Independent firms have already reported greater difficulty in getting bank loans since the announcement of the restructuring.
Governments will be able to distort the free market system and their criteria for assistance programs in favour of their own companies. The federal Government must ensure that independent fish processors retain their share of the industry and remain prosperous to be capable of buying back the industry in the natural process of expansion. The federal

Government must follow its agreement to return the fishing industry to private ownership as soon as possible.
The restructuring of the fishing industry is a mixed blessing. While it restores needed employment in Newfoundland and offers a chance for greater provincial participation in the fishery, it also creates a situation which may lead to greater nationalization of the industry, worse economic performance and a greater dependence on Government subsidies.
The Maritime Provinces and Quebec are opposed to the federal intervention evident in the restructuring plan. These Provinces are concerned about the effects on the independent businessman and the future of these people in the fishing industry. Some Provinces are strongly opposed to the restructuring while others are reluctantly participating because they fear federal reprisals in the form of reduced quotas and expenditures.
In Nova Scotia, the largest fish processor in Atlantic Canada, H.B. Nickerson and Sons, Ltd. is to be dismantled and most of its assets turned over to National Sea Products, making that company the largest in Atlantic Canada. The amalgamation of Nova Scotia's two largest fish processing companies shows that the Governments are more interested in rescuing large corporations than in protecting the livelihood of fishermen, plant workers and small processors.
The Province of Quebec is strongly opposed to the restructuring due to federal intervention in the fishing industry. The industry is rallying fishermen and other groups to oppose the plan and is offering various types of assistance to companies or co-ops that wish to remain independent. Their main objection is that the federal plan would interrupt and delay the provincial program for plant modernization and product quality improvement. The federal Government's plan would interfere with privatization that is now taking place in the Quebec fishing industry.
Nova Scotia has agreed to take part in the restructuring largely because it fears federal reprisals in the form of reduced quotas, reduced small craft harbours funding and other types of discrimination. The Province has not signed the actual agreement as it is seeking stronger guarantees on matters such as returning the controlling interest to the private sector within a specific time. The major objections for Nova Scotia are that about 90 per cent of federal investment in the new company would go directly to repay the bank, leaving little for real industrial rebuilding; federal control in the companies; and an insecure future.
New Brunswick is also opposed to the federal Government controlling interest in fishery enterprises and the effect of the restructured companies upon independents. The industry in New Brunswick also sees a conflict of interest when it comes to distributing fish quotas, subsidies, funding and so on.
In my own Province of Prince Edward Island, the fishermen and people generally are opposed to another form of the old absentee landlord system. They fear that there will be a loss of local decision-making in the fishing industry with a negative effect on the Prince Edward Island independent companies.
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act They are not confident that the federal Government will look after the interests of the P.E.l. fishing industry as it will have to meet demands of larger companies and Provinces, and the larger companies will be given more preference than the independent processors in matters of loan guarantees, subsidies, etc.
The main concern can be summed up in the lack of confidence in the federal Government's handling of an industry which is so important to the livelihood of the Province and indeed to all the Maritime Provinces. It is the lack of trust that makes the Provinces so leery of the whole restructuring plan as the Government has a tendency to change parts of an agreement to suit the needs of the federal Government. An example of this is the way the federal Government has changed the Kirby report. It took a very detailed and comprehensive report and changed portions of it to suit its needs.
While understanding the need for restructuring the Atlantic coast fisheries, one can see that the current action of the federal Government will only create more problems as it tries to nationalize the fishing industry. Do not be fooled when the federal Government says that this is not a plan to nationalize the fishing industry. 1 personally believe that this is a federal Government plan to nationalize the industry. First, it will nationalize the Atlantic fishery and then move to the West Coast next year and nationalize the West Coast fishery as well.
I am most concerned about the smaller businesses. We do not have any large companies in the fishing industry in Prince Edward island that are suffering financially and about to go bankrupt. In Prince Edward Island there are fish processors, family-owned companies, and there are co-ops owned by the fishermen. Most of these companies are surviving though not as well as they would like. Elowever, they are still in business and are not looking for Government bailouts. They are concerned about the restructuring of the Atlantic fishery because they fear that the Government controlled fishing companies will squeeze them out of business. They are also afraid to come to Ottawa to present their concerns in front of the standing committee. I suggest it is a sad state of affairs when citizens of this country are afraid to come to Ottawa to voice their concerns to the Government.

In fact, in 1982, with a total allowable catch in the Gulf of 31,000 metric tonnes, the total fishing capacity of
the Gulf-based fleet caught only 26,000 metric tonnes. They were not able to catch the amount of fish there for the catching because the fish were not there to catch.

Does that indicate, Mr. Speaker, that there is a surplus of fish in the Gulf? The other concern which the independents have is the marketing approach and the countervailing U.S. tariffs that may be applied if this company is set up and the U.S. sees it as a heavily subsidized Government-operated company.
1 see you are indicating that my time is up, Mr. Speaker; I will conclude quickly. The bottom line in this Bill, as far as my appraisal of it is concerned, is purely and simply that there are just too many "anys" in this Bill. I have counted them and would you believe, Mr. Speaker, that there are 13 "anys" in the Bill? Those "anys" give the Government power to do anything it wants to do. Thirteen is a very unlucky number. it is my intention to put forward at a later time an amendment that could possibly be of help. If that particular vehicle is not the answer, I hope some other mechanism can be found. Until such other mechanism is found, I can only stand behind what the Kirby report has recommended.
In conclusion, I would like to say that I support this particular Bill. I believe it should be speedily passed by the House because it is extremely important to our Province. The fishery is the mainstay of Newfoundland. Possibly it is not the most lucrative industry that we have, but it is the most important in terms of culture and heritage as well as economically. The communities in rural Newfoundland and Labrador which are based on the fishery capture the heritage that has been passed on to us from the past. Without a strong fishing industry the very communities that give Newfoundland its unique culture and flavour would be very severely jeopardized. I hope this Bill can get speedy passage and this restructuring idea can be put into practice very swiftly indeed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there Hon. Members seeking to ask questions of the Hon. Member who has just spoken?

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in the idea put forward by the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) that he would like to see a northern fisheries development corporation put in to effect to look after the fishing industry off the coast of Labrador and possibly northern Newfoundland. Could the Hon. Member elaborate on the way that such a corporation might be controlled? Who would sit on its board of directors? Does he envisage both provincial and federal membership? If such an organization ever came into being, how would it be financed? How much money is he looking for? Is it $50 million or $100 million? Where would that money come from? Would some of it come from the fishing operators? Would some of it come from the Province? What would he expect the federal Government to put into the kitty?
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that question was asked. The Government of Canada has already approved $15 million for the capitalization of this new venture. Although it has not yet gone through all of the Government channels that money has been approved by the Government of Canada and is ready to be spent on the capitalization of this new company once approval has been received. It is understood that plants would have to be bought and upgrading would have to be done.
The details regarding how it would operate have not been worked out. We are talking about the principle of setting up a northern development corporation. I can give an example of how the Canadian Saltfish Corporation has operated in the past, and that is to use agents. The Canadian Saltfish Corporation has operated as a clearing house for agents in the private sector up to the present time..It has told small companies that if they catch and process saltfish they will be the agents of the Canadian Saltfish Corporation and the Corporation will buy it from them. The Corporation will market the fish and if it gets a better price than it pays the fishermen, that money goes back to the actual fishermen involved.
I think the fishermen in Newfoundland would say that the Canadian Saltfish Corporation has been a blessing to them. All through this time when the fishery itself was suffering severely, the Canadian Saltfish Corporation and saltfish market was a positive force in the fishery in Newfoundland. In 1982 the Canadian Saltfish Corporation ran the plant at St. Anthony. It had a subsidiary company. Although we did not have an actual board of directors from the community, there was an advisory group in the community that advised the Saltfish Corporation.
I would be open and flexible regarding how this would operate. I fully support the idea of the Government of Newfoundland having a say in this because fish plants are a provincial operation. I welcome the co-operation that we have seen between the two Governments. I would not want to see it dissipate. I believe there are ways of ensuring that the provincial voice is heard in the operation of this particular company.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey). My question relates to that underlying misgiving that I detected in his comments relating to the uncertainty of the role that the individual processor can have under this Bill.
Given the deplorable record of his Government in handling the fisheries problems off the East Coast, what gives him any encouragement at all to feel that under this Bill, where there is nothing explicit in this regard, due account will be made for these individual processors? I would like to hear his comments. I suspect that he has real misgivings here that the Government may not take into account the proper role of the individual processor?

Mr. Speaker, my approach is to fight one battle at a time. I do not think we can solve all of the problems

November 18, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act today. I believe we have laboured long and hard to get where we are today.
I said that this Bill is not perfect but it is the best that we can do. It is the best that the human mind could come up with and the best on which two Governments could agree. It is a step we had to take today and 1 think we should take it quickly because I believe it is important for the industry in Newfoundland.
It does not answer all the concerns. I do have concerns about the small, independent processors. However, 1 will say that they have survived in the past in spite of the fact that we know what has happened to the larger companies. 1 think the Government of Canada has been cognizant of their operations and indeed I know specific instances where Government programs were used to support the small, independent processors.
I do have some concerns. 1 do not believe that all my concerns are answered today by this Bill but that is a battle we will have to fight at a later time. All of us who are concerned about those small, independent processors will have to make sure that within the mechanism that is set up and within Government policy generally, those small processors who have survived and have given employment to small communities are not left out in the cold but are looked after. I believe that very firmly and strongly.
I make the commitment to the Hon. Member that I, for one, will see to it in the days to come that their interests are not neglected but indeed very much looked after.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in hearing the Hon. Member from Newfoundland talk about the importance of the fisheries in terms of the heritage of Newfoundland, the importance of these corporations and agencies and why we in Parliament should be very supportive of him.
My brief comment is that 1 am just a farm boy from the Prairies and I do not know much about fish. However, I support what he says and the way he said it with respect to the necessity to recognize this as an important part of the heritage of the people of Newfoundland. I am hopeful that the House will be very supportive of helping the fishermen.
Why did he not support us when we talked about the importance of the Crow rate to the heritage of the Prairies? Why did we not get the same kind of support from him? 1 put that in the form of a question because I am curious why we could not persuade him to support us for something that was very important to the heritage of our country and to what our pioneers built? Why was the Member not very supportive of us and would he be more supportive of us in the future?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: One short comment because time is almost up.

Mr. Speaker, I do not care what the Edmonton paper says; 1 want to know what the Member feels because 1 would like to support him and what is important to his heritage. 1 want to know how he feels as a Member about my heritage and my part of the country.

Mr. Speaker, in order to accomplish things in the long term sometimes tough decisions must be taken which are painful in the short term. We have experienced this in the Atlantic region. I can tell the Hon. Member that in the same way he may feel some people are experiencing this in the West, we have seen changes in CN Express in Newfoundland. We have seen some changes in the marine coastal operations. We have also seen a lot of improvements. We in the Atlantic Provinces feel that we should be putting our money into what is important in the long term for our area. While that may cause some change and short-term pain, 1 believe in the long term that the politics that are put into place will be beneficial.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for that exchange which took place just now because I think we must regard this particular legislation in the same way as the Prairies regarded the Crow Bill. Fisheries and fish are to the East Coast, and particularly to Labrador, what grain and grain shipment are to the Prairies. There is no question about that in my mind.
Whether this Bill is doing the right thing or not is another matter but it is an important Bill. 1 call Bill C-170 the FishCan Bill because I think we are looking toward the emergence of a creature of Crown proportions which we might call FishCan. My initial comments on this Bill relate to the unusual form which this Bill takes. I do not know how many Members have noticed that it is almost in the form of a resolution rather like the Constitution with all its "whereases". In fact, there are four whereas clauses before we come to the Bill's short title. 1 examined a couple of Bills in the consolidated statutes to see whether there is any parallel to other legislation. It may very well be that when this Bill is published in the Statutes of Canada, the preamble will vanish and it will begin with the short title. However, I still find it rather unusual that there should be these reasons for bringing
November 18, 1983

the Bill forward through the "whereas clauses". I hope the Minister or some other Member opposite will be able to explain that to us. This Bill has been brought forward in an unusual form.
I wish to confine myself to three or four comments on specific areas related to this Bill. My first comment concerns a caution that we must all bear in mind. We are seeing emerge from this Bill a monstrous creature of two Governments which, by what must be a very formal agreement, are deciding to act in concert for the salvation of an important industry. During the preparation of my speech I saw in the material the notion that this Bill is not going to create a Crown corporation. I find that extremely difficult to understand. Perhaps it is a two-Crown corporation since the federal and the provincial Governments are entering into the agreement together. It will have to be a double Crown corporation similar to the dual monarchy in the Austrian-Hungarian empire. Perhaps that is why I have read that it will not be a Crown corporation.
Nevertheless, the manner in which this particular creature of Governments will be acting will be similar to a Crown corporation. This leads me to the conclusion and fear that this may just be a model for something that is going to come about on the West Coast as well.
In this connection I would draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the reply made yesterday by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) to a question put to him by the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller). As reported at page 28940 of Hansard, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans replied to that question as follows:
1 hope that early in the new year I will be able to put before cabinet an important program to give a new start to the Pacific fisheries, exactly as we have been doing for the Atlantic fisheries.
I am sure the NDP will be delighted at this particular operation. It looks very much as though we are going to have two Crown corporations, one on the East Coast and one on the West Coast. I think though that it will be done in the face of a great deal of opposition.
The direction by Governments of industries of this sort is contrary to the whole philosophy of the fishermen on the West Coast. I speak with some knowledge of one particular group, and I venture to say that even the UFAWU might have some misgivings at being bunched under the same Crown with a number of other enterprisers in that part of Canada in an effort to model, direct, control and put fisheries into a common mould on the West Coast. I wonder how, given the dreadful record of this Government in managing anything in the enterprise field, it should have the temerity to stand before us and bring forward another management technique. However, it was a decision in many respects, I suppose, which was forced upon them by the consequences of past performance. I will come to that in a few minutes. In order to bail itself out and to bail out those enterprises which the Government has virtually destroyed, it has had to resort to this particular means.
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
I do think it is worth entering a word of caution at this stage about the impact and the long-term significance of a move of this sort-the creation of a Crown corporation, with virtually unlimited powers, to enter a field of enterprise.
My next comment relates to a peculiar what I think must be described as a conflict, if not of laws, at least a conflict of Bills. In Bill C-170 we have the proposal that the federal and provincial Governments enter into agreements to run a fisheries enterprise. They are doing this in any manner that results in control in fact, whether directly through the ownership of shares, stocks, equity or securities. In other words, there will be an equity position of Governments in this operation.
I see in the Newfoundland agreement, the only one so far of which there is any text, that the proportions as between the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland of the common shares of the enterprise shall be for the Government of Canada to hold 60 per cent and for the Government of Newfoundland to hold 25 per cent, with the remainder partly being held by the Bank of Nova Scotia and a small proportion being held by the employees. More employee participation would obviously be welcomed. But the point I am trying to make-and I think this needs to be underlined-is that the Government of Canada, once the restructuring is completed, will hold the shares in the proportion of 60 per cent, with 20 per cent held by the Government of Newfoundland. That is as foreseen by an agreement that will depend on Bill C-170.
I have before me Bill S-31 which we shall be seeing, no doubt, in the not too distant future. I would like to read Clause 3 of that Bill into the record because it deals with limitations. It reads as follows:
Subject to section 6, no government shall hold or beneficially own more than ten per cent of the shares of any class of shares of a corporation.
Let me point out that the Bill states 10 per cent. We are talking on the one hand of 60 per cent ownership by the federal Government and 25 per cent ownership by the Government of Newfoundland in Bill C-170. But here is Bill S-31 which has a specific purpose in mind, but it has limitations of ownership in any corporation and any Government. The definitions make that quite clear as follows:
"government" means Her Majesty in right of a province and includes
(a)	an agent of Her Majesty in that right, and
(b)	a body corporate that is controlled by Her Majesty in that right.
That limits that Government's participation to 10 per cent. We are talking about an agreement that has already been concluded, according to the Government of Newfoundland, giving a 25 per cent share in this enterprise. I have a funny feeling that this Government does not know what it is doing. Its right hand does not know what its left hand is doing. Mainly it is left-handed; I mean that in the philosophical sense. I am not talking about ambidexterity at all; I am talking about philosophical leftists. That is the problem. I guess it has two left hands and one of the left hands does not know what the other one is doing.
Ten per cent as against 25 per cent causes me considerable concern, Mr. Speaker. We will in the course of time, no doubt,

November 18, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act be asked to look at Bill S-31. Unless we are aware that Bill C-170 has already accorded to a Government a holding of more than 10 per cent in a corporation, then we may just blunder into accepting S-31 without thinking.
There is one proviso we have to recognize also. This is the other side of the story; it is to be found in Clause 6. Clause 3 does say "subject to Section 6". Clause 6(2) of Bill S-31 reads:
The Governor in Council may by order declare that setion 3 or 5 or both shall not apply in respect of any corporation or class of corporations specified in the order.
Section 3 above referred to is Clause 3 I read earlier. The Governor in Council "may" order. In other words, this is not going to be a parliamentary decision; this will be a Government decision. If Bill S-31 were to be passed and be matched side by side with Bill C-170, we would find that the Government would eventually catch up to itself and that it had passed some inconsistent legislation. Then, without reference to Parliament, it will by order declare that Clause 3 shall not apply. This is a danger which I think is worth drawing attention to.
My next comment relates to international agreements. I noticed something in the agreement worked out with Newfoundland, and this is drawn from a press release issued by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans dated October 31. There is provision in the agreement the federal Government worked out with the Province of Newfoundland for the creation of a resources utilization task force composed of equal representation from the two levels of Government. One of the prime objectives of the mandate of this task force will be to review and report upon, first, the displacement of foreign fishing effort and, second, the harvesting of underutilized species and the development of markets for those species.
This takes us back a few years to the days just before the unilateral declaration by the Government-and it is an honourable declaration-of a 200-mile exclusive economic zone, in particular the 200-mile fishing zone. Prior to that declaration there was forethought; there is no question about that. However, what was behind the conclusion of the agreements with foreign countries for the exploitation of stocks, particularly on the East Coast, was the assurance that the countries with which Canada was concluding agreements would be on the same side as Canada in the discussions relating to the Law of the Sea Conference. That was a worthy objective.
What happened in order to buy that support for subsequent meetings of the Law of the Sea, which is very important to us, was that certain countries, some for historic reasons and some for perhaps philosophical reasons, were granted authority to fish stocks in our waters within the 200-mile limit, stocks which were not utilized by Canadian offshore fishermen. 1 am speaking only of the East Coast at the moment. It may be of interest to Hon. Members opposite, who may not have looked into the matter very deeply, to learn that the countries with which Canada concluded agreements to use surplus stocks and stocks Canadians did not use, did not have to process them in Canada. I will come back to that in a moment, but they were
to take off the stock for use in their own countries or for use in barter deals with third countries.
The countries with which Canada made arrangements at that time were Bulgaria, Cuba, the German Democratic Republic, Poland and Romania, an interesting collection. In addition, of course, there were the historical fishermen off the East Coast-Denmark, France, United Kingdom, Portugal and Spain. Probably Portugal and Spain were fishing off the East Coast before any Canadians were here. They had their historical rights. As for Romania, I wonder. Was Romania fishing there before Canada was settled? Was Bulgaria fishing there before Canada was settled? What about Cuba? Perhaps Cuba, through Spain, was fishing there. Were the German Democratic Republic and Poland fishing off the East Coast before Canada was settled?
The German Democratic Republic was looking for red snappers.

That is probably what they were after. As a matter of fact, they were fishing for capelin and other unused and surplus stocks. What was forgotten in the conclusion of those agreements was that once those surplus stocks were caught, they should have been brought to the mainland or to Newfoundland to be processed. That is part of the dismal record of the Government. It did not ensure that what was caught in our waters was processed on our shores. Now we find that it has to resort to extraordinary devices such as dual Crown corporations which have been devised in order to rescue an ailing but important industry.
I do not deny-and I mentioned it right at the beginning- that the fishing industry on the East Coast is extremely important, as it is on the West Coast. However, I am talking mainly about the East Coast because we are dealing with an East Coast matter. This is another aspect of the Bill which has not been given proper attention. Are you feeling uneasy, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro). I was very interested in his presentation and in the facts to which he referred about the amounts of Canadian fish being taken by countries that cannot claim to have historic fishing rights off Newfoundland, countries such as Bulgaria and Romania. Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) for his
November 18, 1983

question. It would not be an easy matter to abrogate treaties. 1 do not think treaties can be abrogated. Canada has no tradition of abrogating treaties. However, the treaties are for a term and when they come up for renegotiation, the most suitable manner of renegotiating them would be to allow the take to continue, provided the processing was done on Canadian territory.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have just a short question for the Hon. Member. It follows on the heels of something which he raised. It deals with the matter of putting their position on the record. We probably share some common positions on the matter. However, since he raised it and since there are many outstanding issues, would the Hon. Member put on the record his Party's position on cancellation of B fishing licences? What kind of action would his Party take against chartered banks that have been very difficult on fishermen over the last couple of years with vessel seizures in some of the most nefarious circumstances which could be conjured up?
What is its position on the removal of such things as the punitive tax on fuel which is extremely difficult for fishermen? What position has his Party put forward on that? What is its position on the delay in providing adequate harbour facilities? As he knows, the fishing industry is under tremendous strain. What is his Party's position on icing facilities, harbour and mooring facilities? We know its position on restraint, but where does it stand on assisting and developing the economy? What is his position on fleet reduction and fleet structure when the reduction is complete? Finally, what is the position of his Party on royalty and the proposal for finnage tax? The previous speaker did raise the spectre of parallels between East Coast solutions and West Coast solutions. His Party had better put some of those positions on the record very quickly so that people can make judgments.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. My friend from the New Democratic Party is, of course, playing a game this afternoon. This is a very serious debate on a Bill which is designed to alleviate a crisis situation in Atlantic Canada. The question that my NDP friend from the West Coast of British Columbia is asking of my colleague who just spoke has almost no relevance whatsoever to what we are discussing today. He knows perfectly well that on all of those questions there has been plenty of evidence in committee and in other places and at meetings I have attended as well as press releases I have made on the West Coast which has given adequate answers. I urge, Mr. Speaker, that you exercise your prerogative and rule him out of order.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.

flippant and frivolous manner. If they continue to do that, they should put up or shut up on the issue.

Don't flounder now.
