For debate, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I was concerned that the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) was standing both this morning and again this afternoon. I do not have in front of me a list of speakers. If the Hon. Member for Western Arctic is agreeable, I will recognize the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway. I am reminded that earlier today I indicated that there would be two Official Opposition speakers as a result of the consent that was given in the House. Perhaps I should look the other way. I will ask the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway to stand down for a moment and I will recognize, pursuant to the agreement made earlier today, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic.

Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that I enter this debate unhampered by any degree of first-hand knowledge of the issue we are discussing. Therefore, 1 can assure you that my views will be entirely objective. 1 also want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that despite my name being Nickerson, I have absolutely no conflict of interest with this Bill. As far as I know, I have no relationship with the well-renowned Nickersons of Nova Scotia who have had a long and honourable association with the fisheries business. In discussing the Bill before us today, Bill C-170, which seeks to facilitate the reorganization of the Atlantic Fisheries, I want to go back a bit in history.
Canada is extremely well endowed with natural resources. Not only do we have fish on the East Coast, West Coast and the inland areas, we also have minerals, oil and gas and a lot of good agricultural land. Despite this endowment by nature, we are not the world's wealthiest country, which we should be. I suspect that our climatic conditions may have a little bit to do with this, but I am sure that the main reason in the other resource industries is the same as in the fishing industry, namely that we have been pursuing the wrong policies for

November 18, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act many years. The Government of the day always wants to concentrate on those sexy industries in central Canada.
We get carried away with computers and microchip technology and forget that probably the real wealth of Canada is in the resource industries, agriculture, timber husbandry, mineral development and, the matter we are discussing today, fisheries. Europeans first came to Canadian East Coast waters in the sixteenth century, I believe, to exploit the fantastic potential of the fisheries in that area. They have been there ever since.
Just a few years ago on the occasion of the extension of Canada's fishing boundary up to the 200-mile limit, 1 remember reading in publications such as the Financial Post that the future of the Canadian East Coast was assured because these moves had been taken. It looked like that part of the country was to become the most wealthy part of Canada. I wonder why this never took place. It never worked out the way the predictions said it would happen.
I guess that costs continued to escalate in large part because of the Government's inflationary policy, high interest rate policy and taxation on petroleum products, which are so important to the fishery, and also because of its high income tax on fishermen. The Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey), who I would have suspected would have had the best interests of fishermen at heart when he was Minister of National Revenue, came down harder than any previous Minister of National Revenue in Canada on the fishermen whom he represented. Therefore the costs have increased.
The market demand for the products of the East Coast fishery unfortunately has not escalated in the way we had hoped. Perhaps some of the problems brought to light by my friend, the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), such as the continued volume of East Coast fish being taken by foreign competitors, has something to do with that. Because the market demand has not been there, prices have not risen as we anticipated. In fact, they decreased considerably in many instances.
My colleagues from the East Coast described the failure of the Liberal Government fisheries policy much better than 1 could do. They demonstrated in this House how these failures of Liberal policy have exacerbated a bad market situation. We come to the present time where the major part of East Coast fishery, the deep sea industry and the operators of large plants, are bankrupt to all intents and purposes. Faced with this question, what is it that a Government should do? I guess that if we could look at this in strictly academic terms and run the whole fisheries of Canada out of the building across the way from here and did not have to bother with the social issues the way they should be faced, the Government would have to do very little or nothing. We could let the fishing companies, the processors and the banks take their losses. I suspect that after awhile, the industry would reorganize itself. It would not need a Bill from this House. Somebody would eventually come along and buy out the assets at ten cents on the dollar or whatever the market value of those assets were. Some of the
smaller marginal plants would probably be closed down and the purchaser would get the industry going again. Perhaps some of successful smaller companies that exist at the present time would take over some of the plants that are not operated economically by the larger companies.
It is unfortunate but true that we cannot allow that to happen. I do not think any Government of Canada could allow that to happen because, Sir, the social consequences would be disastrous. I listened carefully to the speech made by the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Tobin) yesterday, and I am convinced that what he said could happen in those parts of Newfoundland that he represents would come true were the Government to do nothing. Therefore, the Government must do something and must be seen to be trying to do something.
The plan that we have before us now would see possibly two large fish companies coming into existence with part Government ownership at the provincial and federal levels in which the bank and the fishing companies would have some interest. It would appear that an agreement has been reached in the case of the Province of Newfoundland, but unfortunately it appears that negotiations have already broken down with the Province of Nova Scotia.
I have listened to the debate so far in the House, Mr. Speaker, and I have found it quite interesting. It is a debate that has not broken down along Party lines. It has broken down along geographic lines with Hon. Members representing the deep sea areas where these large companies operate generally being very supportive of the Bill. The two Hon. Members who represent the constituencies of St. John's East and St. John's West, for instance, and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries have spoken in favour of the Bill. We on this side of the House have listened to those arguments and see the reason in them. For those reasons, we will not oppose this Bill on second reading.
However, we on this side of the House have also listened to Members such as the Hon. Member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr) and several Hon. Members from Prince Edward Island on both sides of the House. We have listened to the Hon. Members for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), South Shore (Mr. Crouse) and South West Nova (Miss Campbell). The Hon. Member for South West Nova was extremely vocal on this issue yesterday. These Hon. Members representing the inshore areas and the small plant areas have a very different perception of the Bill.
The people in those areas are scared of what might result from this Bill if it is taken to its logical conclusion in the years to follow. They see a very large Government backed competitor possibly becoming a monopoly. They see these large organizations having a great power in the marketplace that is not available to the smaller operators. I can see that possibly, a couple of years down the road, the Government will be coming back to the House of Commons asking for an exclusive monopoly on marketing by these corporations. I certainly
November 18, 1983

would be very scared of that if 1 were a small fisherman or small plant owner or operator.
The Government, Sir, controls all of the rules of the game in the fishing business. It controls the quotas and the regulations governing the way in which one might fish. The Government decides where improvements such as wharves and harbours might be built. This would cause me great concern were 1 to be a small fisherman or small fish plant operator. Those small fishermen and small fish plant operators are scared of the competition from highly subsidized Government backed competitors.
In a way it is ironic, or perhaps it shows how the market system operates fairly well when left alone, that many of these small operators, even with today's depressed prices, have still been successful, especially those who concentrate their business on a selected area of the market. We have heard of the experience of plants specializing in lobsters or scallops, for instance.
I believe that the fears voiced by these people are fully justified. 1 have had some experience with the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. The experience we have had in the West and the North is that when the Government first comes in, it is not satisfied until it gets full control of the market. It keeps getting a little bit more and a little bit more control until it ends up with a full and complete monopoly. All of the small fish buyers in my constituency were swallowed up by this Crown corporation and the industry has been nationalized. The fisherman has no alternative but to sell his product to the nationalized company at the prices it dictates. There is no freedom left in the industry.
If the Liberals stay in office in this country, and I do not believe there is much of a possibility for that to happen, then I am sure that what has happened with the FFMC would also happen on the East Coast. This, Sir, is feared by many, including myself, as being the first step in a wholesale nationalization of the East Coast industry. If 1 have time, toward the end of my presentation I will make suggestions for possible amendments to the Bill which would see that these worst fears will not be realized.
As well, Sir, judging by the experience 1 have had with the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, I can guarantee that nobody but nobody is worse at selling fish than those in the Government. Bureaucrats simply cannot sell fish. They are not equipped to sell fish. There is no way that they can sell fish.
There was once a viable industry in the Slave Lake area of my constituency. People went fishing in that lake and in the inland lakes nearby with the idea that they could make money, and they usually did. However, since the Government took the industry over, there is no longer a viable industry. It is entirely dependent upon subsidies. If those subsidies were to be taken away, the industry would die overnight. It is more like a welfare system than it is like a living industry at the present time. I would not want to see that happen to our friends on the East Coast of Canada.
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
The plan that is now before us was described by the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) as being the lesser of many evils, and I am inclined toward that way of thinking. If we must accept that plan, then let us examine the Bill to see if it does what the Government says it is designed to do or if it can be improved. My first observation is that this is a typical Liberal Bill. It is designed to grant the Government wide-sweeping powers. The Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) spoke about these powers in a great deal of detail so I will not repeat what he said.
The Bill seeks to give the Government virtually carte blanche authority to do anything the Government wants with the East Coast fishery industry. Not only that, Sir, the Bill goes on forever and ever. The authority that the Government is seeking from Parliament never comes to an end but goes on forever. The Government says it needs extraordinary powers in order to reorganize the fisheries at the present time, but this Bill would give the Government those powers forever. The Government would have those powers not simply in the case of the present emergency but forever and ever. 1 think that that is unacceptable.
This Bill needs a very critical examination in committee. For instance, Subclause 8(1) gives the Government authority to invest up to $138 million until March 31, 1985. However, if we look at Subclause (2), we will find that there is no limit in the future. The Government can go through the normal Appropriation Act procedure whereby that Act is deemed to have been approved even if we do not debate it in the House for five minutes. So there is no real control over those appropriations. Government can come back in 1986 and put $300 million into it, and the following year a billion dollars, and there is nothing that Parliament can do.
I believe there has to be within this Bill a guaranteed maximum spending limit so that if the Government wants to exceed that, it has to come back to Parliament. I am pleased to see there is a limit on the amount of guarantees it can make. However, in my opinion, a limit should certainly be there in respect of the amount of cash it can spend and invest. To assuage the fear of back door nationalization, which has been spelled out by those Members who represent the smaller aspect of the industry, there should be within this Bill a specified limit of Government participation in any one of these entities which they intend to create.
My last point is that if we look at the Bill in its present form, it is like a lobster trap. We can get into it very easily, Sir, but it is going to be very difficult ever to get out unless we make the necessary amendments. There must be a way specified within the Bill as to the way it will end and the way we can get the East Coast fishing industry back into private hands where it really belongs. I would foresee a schedule laid out in the Act where the maximum participation which I mentioned previously would decline over a number of years. There would be a declining maximum participation specified over a period of a number of years.

November 18, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
Most important, there must be a termination date as to when the authority, which the Government is asking be granted to it by Parliament, comes to an end. By that date, the Government should make sure that the industry is returned to private hands and that the state no longer has an equity position in the East Coast fishery.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could say right away that I find it very ironic that what we are really faced with here is a Bill which nationalizes a very troubled East Coast fishing industry, at least the major part of the industry, creating the largest fish company in the world out of the rubble of the Nickerson National Sea empire. This is done by a Liberal Minister and that famous or infamous wheeler-dealer, Mr. Michael Kirby, and by two Conservative Premiers in Nova Scotia and in Newfoundland, and which is supported in the House today by the Conservative Party. I find it ironic because if we in the New Democratic Party were to do that, we would be condemned for being nasty socialists who were nationalizing a troubled company. Yet here are all these Hon. Members supporting this Bill.
1 believe the Bill is a good idea and 1 am going to say something about that in my remarks. However, I want to say right away, Mr. Speaker, that, as the last speaker admitted at the beginning of his speech, 1 also am not an expert on fish. I am a long way away from being an expert in the fisheries. As a matter of fact, my riding is probably the only riding in the Lower Mainland of British Columbia which does not front on the ocean. However, 1 did want to say a few words today because 1 am very sympathetic to the Atlantic Canada region.
I find certain similarities with my area of the country, namely, British Columbia. It is a region where one industry dominates, as in our part of the country where we have the forest and mining industries.
1 can sympathize with the people of Atlantic Canada who, I am told, out of a population of two million, have about 100,000 directly employed in the fishing industry. Of course, many other people are employed as a result of spin-offs from the fishing industry. If you consider that there are nine million people in Ontario and about 75,000 are auto workers, which is one of the major industries in Ontario, you can understand how important the fishing industry is in terms of people being employed in Atlantic Canada. There is an additional problem in Atlantic Canada. If you look, Mr. Speaker, at the eastern seaboard of the United States, you find that people who are fishing there, when fishing is difficult, can always quit and go and work in manufacturing, then come back to the fishery a few years later. You cannot do that in Atlantic Canada because of the general economy there and the lack of a manufacturing base. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I understand that when you close a fish plant, just as when you close a mine or a pulp mill in British Columbia, it means a death sentence to a community.
I would like to ask why the fishing industry is in trouble. Why is it-if you will pardon the pun-floundering on a sea of red ink? I feel there are a number of reasons and I would like to go through them. I think there were tremendous expectations which came about because of the extension of the 200-mile limit. The result was overcapitalization in the industry. Another reason was the recession of 1980 which resulted in fewer products being sold and in lower prices to the fishermen. Therefore, there was a decline in sales and a decline in prices. 1 believe also that part of it was due to a management position to expand even at the beginning of tough times. Perhaps the reason was over-optimism, furthered by the hope of getting Government grants and so on.
The Liberal Government must bear some of the responsibilities for the difficulty in the industry, and the Conservative Government before it, because both the Clark Conservative Government and the present Liberal Government favoured high interest rates and monetarist policies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Come on.
The Hon. Member says, "Come on". I ask him to look at the interest rates in this country in the last three years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Look at the height of the sky also.

These high interest rates brought on by the Liberal Government, and the body which it controls, namely, the Bank of Canada, through its appointment of the Governor of the Bank of Canada, really squeezed out any hope that these fishing companies could make a go of it. So while some fishermen could even double their catch, they were tripling their debts and, as you know, Mr. Speaker, you cannot survive if you do that.
I would like to quote from some remarks which were made in this House by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nanai-mo-Alberni (Mr. Miller), who is the fisheries critic for our Party. I quote as follows from page 28,858 of Hansard for November 14, 1983:
Companies had paid little enough attention to increasing the quality of their catch or improving their marketing strategies. This led to a decline in the ability to sell fish and the ability to support the economics of the industry.
What happened then was that the industry in fact collapsed. We then saw a deal between the present Fisheries Ministry, the Premier of Nova Scotia and the Premier of Newfoundland. That odd couple, Ottawa and Newfoundland, finally got together to deal with the fisheries industry. As I understand the Bill, it provides authority for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) to spend $138 million to restructure the groundfish processing sector in eastern Canada. This restructuring is based, as I said, on two agreements, one with Newfoundland and one with Nova Scotia. This will see the creation of two new super companies, the largest in the world, from the dregs of the five major and a few smaller processors. I do not think my colleague was here at the time, but I said that I find it ironic that this is nationalization of part of the
November 18, 1983

industry and while the Conservatives and Liberals are scampering not to say that, they are still supporting it.
The federal Government is going to inject $138 million in cash and hold the majority of shares in each company. The provincial Governments and the Bank of Nova Scotia, by converting debt into equity, will hold minority shareholder positions. Not bad for the Bank of Nova Scotia. Perhaps it gets rid of that tremendous debt on its fisheries account. The Nova Scotia agreement is not completely finalized, but in the Newfoundland agreement there is a potential for employee ownership and a seat for the union on the board of directors. Can you believe it? We might even be getting a little bit of progressive legislation. We might be able to get some legislation where employees of the company will start feeling they are really part of the whole process and will become more productive. That of course is the way to productivity, not by beating them over the head as the Conservative-Social Credit Government of British Columbia tends to do.
We in the NDP will be supporting the Bill, as I gather you have surmised, despite some of the shortcomings which 1 want to go into in a couple of minutes. There is no doubt that some form of intervention was necessary. As 1 said, many smaller communities in eastern Canada are completely reliant on the continued operation of the plants and related fishing activities. We do not see any viable alternative at this particular time. There is some necessity for getting this restructuring in place very soon, before the next fishing season, because sales contracts and renegotiation of the union contract are pending. 1 want to again quote our fisheries critic from his opening speech at page 28858 of Hansard where he said:
It is necessary to proceed with this Bill because the future of the next fishing season in Atlantic Canada relies on it. If this Bill is not passed, if there is not a restructuring of the industry and if a board of directors is not appointed to the new companies in Atlantic Canada, there will be a great deal of uncertainty about markets and our ability to sell the product that is harvested over the next year. As well, the matter of negotiations between the fishermen's unions and the company for contracts in Atlantic Canada depends upon this Bill and suppliers must know whether the debts that are owed to them at the moment will be repaid. There are a great many other uncertainties in almost every community in Atlantic Canada and hundreds and hundreds of those communities are dependent upon the fishing industry.
That is all the more reason why the Bill should go to committee.
1 gather, in following the debate, that the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) brought up the problem of smaller companies which are not included in this deal. I acknowledge that they need some assurance from the Government that they will not be forced out of business. Even a rampant socialist like myself can say that. There also needs to be some concerns about selling off the companies to foreign owners and so on. 1 also think we should not be in any hurry. 1 notice various speakers have talked about this hurry to have the Government bail out the industry, get it going again and then sell it out to private enterprise. If these big companies work, and if the workers in this industry can really feel they are part of the whole thing, that it is not "them and us", it is all "us" in these
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act two large companies, then I would think we would want to continue with these companies. But that is looking into the future and that is difficult to do.
Before I sit down I do want to look into the future at one aspect. We all know Michael Kirby; he is a man who, I suppose, has made as many enemies in Atlantic Canada as he has made deals. But he is to be, if not congratulated, at least we will acknowledge his hard work and sincerity in getting these deals together. It is obviously a lot of hard work because there must be a minefield of competing interests in this area. However, I would like to caution the Government that, when it comes to dealing with the West Coast industry, and the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni and the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) are much more expert on that industry than 1 am, the Government should be very careful in the way it treats the West Coast industry. It is a different kind of industry. If there is to be restructuring there, I ask the Government to do it openly with as much consultation as possible. Put everything on the table, because that is the way to negotiate. 1 would not want to repeat the spectre of the Crow in the sense of Ottawa taking the position, as viewed from western eyes, that Ottawa knows best and therefore we will force whatever restructuring we think the industry needs. I have my nose to the wind and I understand that there are some things about to happen to the industry on the West Coast, perhaps the purchasing of companies and so on, but I just say to the Government that it should be open and above-board and that there should be much consultation.
I think I have touched on all the areas I wanted to. I think the detail can be done in committee, where I hope the Bill will go soon. As someone who lives a long way from Atlantic Canada but who has a great deal of sympathy with what the people there are trying to do and what they are going through in the fishing industry, I wish them luck. They are going to need it. I wish them a future in a really viable industry. While there are problems, 1 think the Bill really sets the basis for doing that. It really is quite a unique opportunity for fishermen in the Provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland to take from this dead, bankrupt industry and build something which can be really viable. All Canadians can be proud of a real working industry there.

Mr. Speaker, I know it is late on a Friday afternoon and perhaps everything that can be said about this Bill on second reading has been said, but I would like to add my comments to what Hon. Members have said in this Chamber.
First of all, there must be an absolutely clear understanding that this Bill must be accepted, perhaps reluctantly, by this House because the Government has put forward nothing else to meet a crisis which has continued now since at least the summer of 1981, and to which the Government has not made any adequate response. This is not to say that this Bill is a perfect Bill. Because the Government waited so long to act, the Bill amounts to a piece of enabling legislation to put into effect one agreement that has been entered into between the federal Government and the Province of Newfoundland and to give

November IB, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act power to implement another agreement which the federal Government hopes to enter into with the Province of Nova Scotia. It also enables the Government to establish a huge national fishing corporation. The bulk of the power to make decisions will rest with the Government, not only because of the structure of that fishing corporation, but because the Government already regulates and controls the resource to which all of the user groups of Atlantic Canada must resort. That is the fishery. The consequence of this is an establishment of immense state power. It is done in response to a crisis. The tragedy is that it is done in response to a crisis for which the Federal Government must take responsibility to a significant extent.
During the summer of 1981 my colleague, the former Minister of Fisheries, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), was warning the Government that action was required. At that time it was quite clear that the companies were not going to be able to carry on for two reasons. The first reason was the difficulty because of markets. The second reason was over-expansion and the extreme difficulty in carrying the loans as a consequence of high interest rates. Those interest rates continued to go up. Those companies and the banks which had made loans to them were in a position where they could not get sufficient cash flow to get out of the difficulties.
During the 1980 elections the Hon. Member who is now the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) said that he would resign rather than belong to a Government that did not bring interest rates down. Tell that to the people in Atlantic Canada.
They were 14 per cent then.
At that time they were 14 per cent, as my hon. colleague points out.
And went up to 24 per cent.

And went up to 24, as another hon. colleague points out. I am sure if 1 stand here for a few minutes, other rates will come to mind. Mr. Speaker, the fact of the matter is that the situation in Atlantic Canada was clearly visible in the summer of 1981. All during that autumn, questions were asked in the House repeatedly. There was a special debate. The Minister of Fisheries at the time kept saying that the situation was not too severe. He was trying to get away from the responsibility that the Government of Canada held by saying it was the fault of the companies, they should not have built so many processing plants. In one speech he said that he had warned the corporations and companies, both large and small. While he was giving the warnings, the Department of Economic Expansion was putting up the money and practically forcing the industry to build the processing plants. The Government of Canada is the Government that controls the fishery and regulates its catch and allotments. It intervenes, and not always to good effect, into the fishery. The result of delay between 1981
and now resulted in a frantic attempt to be seen to be doing something.
In January of 1982 I was in St. John's, Newfoundland. I was asked what the Conservative Government would do if it were in power then. I said that the Atlantic fishery needed then an immediate influx, either through guarantees, loans or some other mechanism, of $100 million to stabilize the industry and to save the industry and the private sector in the industry. Mr. Kirby laughed. He said my figures were excessive. The then Minister of Fisheries laughed and said they had nothing like that amount in mind. Mr. Speaker, this Bill starts off with $138 million. It carries on to guarantees of $100 million. That does not even begin to count the money that has been committed to the Atlantic fishery as a consequence of the Kirby Report some months ago.
Fleet replacement.

Fleet replacement and other things, as is properly pointed out by my hon. friend. Mr. Speaker, in the first week in January of 1982 we, who had an answer that would have retained a viable private fishing industry, were laughed at. We were told they were not even thinking of $100 million. If the Government had acted then there would have been no need for this particular Bill.
Why didn't you act?

As my hon. friend on the Liberal side of the House knows, in January of 1982 we were not the Government. He represented the Government and sat on the Treasury benches. The question is why he and his colleagues did not act. We could not act. The power in this House lay with the Government.
The Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) yesterday said: "There is no need for such a Bill". He was referring to this particular Bill. 1 agree there is no need for this particular Bill, but because of the neglect of his own Government there is need for a Bill. As 1 said at the beginning, we must, with reluctance, accept the passage of this Bill.
My hon. friend, the Liberal Member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell) is from a part of Nova Scotia that understands well the difficulties of and also the opportunities for the Atlantic fishery. She said: "Certainly my constituents feel it will affect them, and they want more information . . . The powers the Bill gives to the Minister seem to be unlimited."
It is all very well for my hon. socialist friend, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), to offer some caveats about the power in this Bill. It is understandable that he does so. While he wants to endorse nationalization, even he understands that the powers in this Bill are quite extraordinary. The Bill, in Clause 4, says the power is:
To carry out the purpose of this Act, the minister may, on behalf of Her Majesty,
(a) acquire, hold or dispose of or otherwise deal with shares, debentures or
other securities of, or any security interest in, any fishery enterprise;
November 18, 1983

This Bill is a Bill to execute and implement one agreement and another that is hoped to be signed by the Government. The Bill does not confine itself just to the subject of the agreements, which are not mentioned in the Bill. It gives power to do these things with other fishery companies which may well not be in financial difficulty at the moment and which we can call the independents. Because of the neglect of the Government over a long period of time something had to be done. The people in Atlantic Canada cannot be thrown out of work completely. Their means of making a living cannot just disintegrate as a consequence of this neglect.
But there is another section of the Atlantic fishery of which other Hon. Members, especially on the Government side, have spoken. That sector views this piece of legislation with concern. They do not want to see fellow fishermen thrown out of work and do not want to see a large part of the Atlantic fishery collapse. They do not want to see it forced to go through a painful process of re-establishment.
They also do not want their viable, effective and competent part of the industry to go under, which is a concern of theirs over the sweeping powers of this Bill. My hon. friend from the NDP commented on this a few minutes ago. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway said that some form of intervention was necessary. I understand that, because I am aware of the political ideology which lies behind that statement. However, even he recognized the concern of the independents. He said, "They need some assurance that they will not be forced out of business". This matter has not only been raised by my colleagues from the NDP who are the advocates of nationalization and socialization but also by my colleagues on the Government side. While they are perhaps more content with intervention and nationalization than some others in the House, they too have raised the concern of fellow fishermen in Atlantic Canada about the extraordinarily immense power of this particular Bill. They have commented that for all practical purposes there is no accountability. While the Hon. Minister can argue that parliamentary approval is required in order to get additional sums, we know that that is not the kind of accountability that is required. What is required is a constant reporting mechanism to the House.
Hon. Members on the Government side also know that the independents in their part of Atlantic Canada are getting clear signals from the banks and the investment community that there will be a diminution of the necessary funds for them to carry on and plan their business affairs until there is a more clear idea of what kind of power might be exercised under this Act.
Since this alarm has been raised by all Members of the House-1 fully compliment my friends on the Liberal side for having the good sense to recognize it for what it is-I hope that those Members from Atlantic Canada on the Government
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
side will come forward at committee stage and assist us in bringing forward some witnesses who will be able to help us perhaps in making amendments which might be necessary to alleviate that concern. I also hope that all Members of the House will address themselves to the question of accountability-
There is another side to this legislation. It is the intention of the Government eventually to reprivatize the capital assets and corporate structure that will be taken over by the Government, at least in the initial stage. It is terribly important that if there is to be any capacity to reprivatize, the independent sector of the Atlantic fishery must not become so frightened or concerned that it ceases to have economic viability to be in a position to help the Government in its stated objectives of reprivatization. Those of us who have put many long days and weeks into the study of the Atlantic fishery and have spoken here on many occasions in support of a viable and effective Atlantic fishery want to be assured that there will be an honest expression of intention made very clear during the committee and further stages of this Bill. We want to be clear that the objective is indeed to withdraw Government intervention as soon as possible.
I think it has been made very clear from the debate so far that all Members of the House, for different reasons, understand that this Bill must now be accepted. I also believe that all Members understand there are some problems with the Bill. For instance, the Hon. Member for Gloucester believes that this Bill should not have been necessary. Although he says it is not necessary now, I believe it is. Perhaps the Bill could be in another form, but something must be done. We do not believe that the situation had to develop to this point but it has, and on behalf of my Party we are saying to all people involved in the Atlantic fishery that we know the Bill must now be accepted and we will do nothing to prevent the Government from doing those things that must be done now to maintain employment and some kind of viability in the Atlantic fishery.
But we must also say to others in Atlantic Canada that we are very conscious indeed that this Bill must be watched carefully. The powers contained in it must be constrained to meet the Government's stated objective eventually to withdraw and allow the Altantic fishery to carry on in a viable and healthy way with as much private initiative as possible.
